The U.S. Constitution vests the President with the power to approve or veto bills that have passed both chambers of Congress, a process governed by the Presentment Clause in Article I, Section 7, Clause 2 [d1, d6, d7]. After a bill is enrolled and presented, the President has up to ten days (excluding Sundays) to sign it into law, veto it and return it with objections, or allow it to become law without a signature; if vetoed, Congress may override the veto by a two‑thirds vote in both the House and Senate [d5, d6, d7]. These facets—presentment, presidential action options, and congressional override—together describe the complete legislative approval/veto framework under the Constitution [d1, d5, d6, d7].
